items.body: Across eight untitled pieces, fold/interval develops a musical language in which guitar dyads, granular electronics, filtered resonances and microscopic digital artefacts coexist within carefully articulated sonic environments. By directing attention towards the behaviour of sound itself, its texture, spectral balance and the constantly shifting relationships between one resonance and the next, Giuseppe Ielasi and Fabio Perletta engage in an open exchange that is equally balanced and coherent. The title of the project itself offers an illuminating point of entry. In audio synthesis, wavefolding is a process in which a signal exceeding a certain threshold is folded back onto itself, generating new harmonics and increasingly complex timbral structures instead of simply clipping or distorting. The second half of the title is equally revealing. Throughout the album, Giuseppe Ielasi’s guitar is reduced to two-note dyads—musical intervals—whose quiet interjections provide the elementary material from which Fabio Perletta’s electronic processes unfold. Fold describes a continuous process of sonic transformation; interval refers both to the guitar’s harmonic vocabulary and to the spaces separating successive sonic events. The music continually inhabits both meanings. The dialogue between Ielasi and Perletta never feels predetermined. Repeated figures evolve through minute changes in density, frequency and perspective, while silence functions as an active compositional force, shaping every gesture with remarkable precision. Listening gradually shifts away from isolated sonic events towards intervals in both senses of the word: the relationships between pitches and the spaces separating sounds. Tiny overtone fluctuations, delicate feedback and almost imperceptible transients continually redefine the surrounding acoustic field. Giulia Bruno‘s photographic contribution is integral to the project. Her images of landscapes, architectural structures and technological infrastructures mirror the music’s fascination with hidden systems, suspended attention and processes unfolding beneath the threshold of immediate perception. Sound and image share the same temporal logic, encouraging prolonged observation rather than instant recognition. Ultimately, fold/interval is a record about relationships: between acoustic and electronic sound, presence and absence, transformation and stasis. Every gesture appears with an acute sense of proportion. Like the wavefolding process evoked in its title, it reveals how complexity can emerge from the continuous reshaping of the simplest materials. giulia bruno (self portrait giulia bruno) To find out more we have spoken directly with Ielasi, Perletta and Bruno. Untitled (1–8) feels poised between presence and absence: Giuseppe’s sparse guitar gestures seem to emerge from and dissolve back into Fabio’s electronic textures, while Giulia’s photographs introduce a parallel visual rhythm. How did the three of you develop a shared language across sound and image, and at what point did the project become more than a musical collaboration and evolve into fold/interval itself? Giulia Bruno: fold/interval was born from the desire to create together within a free and anti-hierarchical relational context, where sounds and images can also follow a shared path, without subordination. Our relationship began with mutual respect and with a friendship that developed over time. Recognizing ourselves in what each of us does — and perhaps also in who each of us is through our work — created a solid foundation from which the desire emerged to explore something unexpected together, grounded in a shared trust in looking and listening. The project therefore arises from the desire to bring together thoughts, sensibilities, and intuitions that find their form through shared sounds, images, and silences. Fabio Perletta: fold/interval was never just a musical project; rather, it started as a trio. Before that, Giuseppe and I had been discussing the possibility of collaborating in a broader sense. Giulia and Giuseppe already knew each other well, having collaborated for a long time, so everything naturally found its way into fold/interval, which was conceived as a space for exchange involving different practices and sensibilities, where sound and image could develop together. We aim to find a shared space where listening and looking can influence each other, and where unexpected connections could emerge. The music and the photographs are not separate layers, but different manifestations of a shared process and vision. Giuseppe Ielasi: I have been working with Giulia, on different projects, for more than 15 years. This was mainly on film or installation works. More recently we started discussing about possible live performances, and our first one as a duo happened in June 2025 at the Triennale in Milano. We loved it, but at the same time felt the need to work on something less structured, more open to improvisation and surprises. I also know Fabio since a long time: we shared a few concerts and he published some of my music on 901editions, but most of all we exchanged thoughts, music and spent a lot of time together in the last years. We were ready for a collaboration and started playing and recording together. It was very natural, then, to merge those projects, introducing Giulia to Fabio. My impression is that the shared language was already there, it was just a matter of making things happen. fabio perletta (photo oyamada kuniya) The release includes photographs ranging from natural and architectural environments to technological infrastructures, including an image of the cooling systems of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. Given the increasing debate around the environmental cost of AI and large-scale computation, were these infrastructures approached primarily as visual forms, or do they also function as reflections on the invisible systems that increasingly shape contemporary life and knowledge production? GB: My work never approaches images solely as visual forms. Rather, the image is a pretext for activation: a way of bringing to light contemporary questions concerning collective issues, research processes, and systems of relation. In this sense, I am interested in deconstructing the aesthetics of the image, removing it from spectacle so that it can become an activator. An activator of processes of change and reflection on how we observe, recognize, and respond to different forms of violence and contradiction. I believe we are often suspended within a constant tension: between hypnosis and impotence, between beauty and fear, between systems of seduction and power and critical awareness. This is why I am interested in working with the landscape — whether natural, technological, architectural, infrastructural, human, or relational — as a space to be read, questioned, and traversed. The infrastructures, and what is reactivated through photography, are therefore not merely formal presences, but signals of broader, often invisible systems that condition the way we live, know, and imagine the future, within an obsessive system of continuous archiving. To look also means asking ourselves what choices we can make in order to build a collectivity capable of coexisting, resisting, and generating new forms of relation. FP: I believe this connection is at the core of fold/interval. The project does not come from a desire to blindly produce new images and sounds, but rather to create a space where attention can be reactivated and where different, heightened forms of perception coexist. We are not interested in spectacularization, our focus is on cultivating attention. The way we work together is based on a process of listening and waiting, allowing each element to emerge without forcing relationships or creating predetermined correspondences. We were drawn to what happens in the space between things: between the visible and the hidden, between what is heard and what is left in silence. In this sense, fold/interval reflects a resistance to the acceleration and saturation that define contemporary production and consumption. This first work seeks to open up a different temporal dimension—one where the viewer and listener are invited to sit with uncertainty, observe the details, and forge their own connections. giuseppe ielasi (photo philip ielasi) The music is remarkably restrained. Guitar notes and chords seem to drift through digital circuitry, leaving large amounts of space between events. Was reduction a conscious compositional strategy from the outset, or did the pieces gradually arrive at this sparse form through a process of subtraction and editing? FP: From my perspective, it is a combination of both. The way Giuseppe and I approach sound within this project stems from a shared interest in creating an environment where every element holds its own weight and presence, allowing unexpected encounters to unfold. Reduction wasn’t a conscious aesthetic choice; it emerged from a desire to let the space breathe and become an active component of the composition. Silence, resonance, and the intervals between events are not mere voids, but structural pillars that give sounds the room to reveal their intrinsic qualities. At the same time, this sparseness was already baked into the sounds we each brought to the table. Giuseppe’s guitar—with its precision and abstract quality—and my stylized electronic textures, which are often pushed toward the extreme areas of the spectrum, come from very different yet complimentary worlds. Throughout the process, we constantly sought an organic balance between these two worlds, letting the clarity and subtle details of the guitar interact with the ambiguity and roughness of the electronics. GI: It’s strange, the music doesn’t feel that restrained to me. There’s constant activity in it, lots of repetitions (but no loops) and the pacing and placing are very deliberate, but somehow the flow feels very natural (the idea of ‘restrain’ somehow suggest that it was ‘forced’, and that is not the case). There was little subtraction, and almost no editing. We suggested basic materials and layers and realized that many of those could co-exist and interacts very naturally. It was a very intuitive, non-formalised process. Giulia, many of your recent texts engage with questions of technological mediation, the overproduction of images, and the difficulty of maintaining spaces of reflection within contemporary systems of visibility. Do you see a connection between those concerns and the aesthetic choices behind Untitled (1–8), which often feels like it is resisting speed, saturation and information overload in favour of slowness, ambiguity and attention? GB: We are connected by a shared way of thinking: the desire not to follow the logics of production, seduction, and spectacularization, but rather the rhythm of our own thought and listening. It is a natural gaze, made of layers but not oversaturation, of words expressed with care, and of a constant search for coherence. There are no predetermined rules or rigid orders of thought, but rather a natural transformation that emerges from the attempt to remove the work from what is immediately displayed. We are interested in what remains suspended, what requires time, what does not immediately offer itself only as an image or as information. The reflection on the macrosystems in which we move as individuals runs through our thinking and our gaze, and also shapes the way we relate to others. Untitled (1–8) emerges from this attention: from the desire to create a space in which sound, image, and word can slow down perception and open up the possibility of a shared rereading of the processes that involve us. FP: I am drawn to the word Giulia mentioned: rhythm. Our biological rhythm—the intrinsic time we need to process our surroundings—differs for everyone, but it is undeniably a means of survival in this violent, vulgar world. To honor it requires welcoming the complex, the unexpected, the unheard, and the unseen. We aim to stay close to this idea, not in a literal, romantic, or strictly political sense, but as a practice that resists the pressure to produce immediate meaning or visibility. Giulia’s reflection on overproduction and the saturation of images deeply informs how we approach both sound and vision: not as materials to be quickly consumed, but as processes demanding time. The project seeks to create a space where perception can remain open and non-finalised, where things are not immediately resolved into information or representation. Instead, it sustains an alternative internal tempo—one that allows for hesitation, repetition, and return. fold/interval is described not only as an audiovisual project but also as a publishing platform. Beyond this first release, how do you envision the project developing? Are future editions likely to continue exploring the relationship between image, sound and material publication, or do you see fold/interval evolving into a broader framework for collaborations, research projects and new commissions? GB: Starting from the coming together of our conversations, we did not want to place any limit on the project’s transformation. We believe in a path made of coherence, but also of responses to research processes that can change, expand, and take on new forms over time, just as we ourselves change over time. For us, collaboration means first and foremost engaging in dialogue and confrontation. We have not placed any limit on this exchange, except for the desire to do it with people who share with us a vision of the world in which aesthetics is never placed above relationships, research, and the search for meaning in life. In this sense, fold/interval may continue to explore the relationship between image, sound, and material publication, but it may also open itself to other forms: collaborations, research, commissions, dialogues, and processes that have not yet been anticipated. What interests us is that it remains a living space, capable of transforming without losing coherence. FP: For me, fold/interval is less of a fixed container and more of an open ecology, inherently built to evolve. The idea of the publishing platform naturally stems from a desire to give a physical, tangible form to time and thought, which is why the material aspect will always remain a core interest. Looking ahead, I imagine fold/interval evolving as a flexible framework that could manifest as a physical edition, a sound installation, a research residency, or simply a space for shared dialogue. Future editions might not always look or sound the same, it will simply follow the needs of the encounters and questions that emerge along the way. GI: What interests me is to collaborate on a project that’s very open, hard to define and might even be confusing at times. We released an edition with a cd and a set of photos, a short film on our website and we’re co-curating some events and sound installations at “settantaventidue” in Milano. But we also exist as a label / publishing platform (more editions, with or without music, might appear soon and those could include other collaborators) and we’re planning some concerts, residencies and installations for the next months. So, yes, it’s definitely evolving and I’m very curious to see what will happen. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: fold/interval 由 Giuseppe Ielasi 与 Fabio Perletta 合作，将吉他的双音音程作为基础材料，融入颗粒合成电子、滤波共振与微观数字声响，构建出八个无标题的声学空间。评论将专辑标题视为理解整张作品的关键线索：wavefolding 指向信号在阈值之上折叠回自身、不断生成新谐波的连续变形过程，而 interval 同时指代吉他双音的音程关系与声音事件之间的留白。音乐在两种含义之间游走，声音事件从不孤立存在，而是在密度、频率与视角的细微变化中持续演化，沉默作为主动的作曲力量参与塑造每一处细节。Giulia Bruno 的摄影以建筑、地景与科技基础设施为对象，与音乐共享同一套时间逻辑——关注隐藏的系统、悬置的注意力与感知阈值之下的过程。整张专辑关注的是关系本身：原声与电子、在场与缺席、变形与静止之间的持续协商，从最简材料中生长出复杂性。

items.body: Atrición is the sort of record that seems to have been built under fluorescent light, with the smell of disinfectant somewhere nearby and history banging its head against the walls. Santiago Nicolás wrote much of it in an oncology center, and that circumstance hangs over the album with a terrible physical clarity. The body here is material: cells change, systems fail, pressure accumulates, and time works patiently on everything it touches. Nicolás places that fact beside political violence, invasion, borders, archives, and inherited trauma, finding a shared logic in processes that advance by occupation and erosion rather than spectacle. That could have produced a record swollen with significance. Instead, Atrición stays severe, compact, and rhythmically exact. Its drums hit with the blunt economy of DAF and Nitzer Ebb, while the synths carry the cold forward motion of contemporary techno. Suicide lurks in the repetition, Cabaret Voltaire in the sense that machinery can become a social instrument, and Schwefelgelb in the clipped, bodily momentum. Nicolás keeps tightening the screws until repetition stops feeling like recurrence and starts behaving like pressure. This is where the album becomes genuinely nasty in the best sense. A beat returns, a distorted percussion figure acquires another layer, a synthesizer line keeps digging into the same patch of ground, and suddenly you understand accumulation as an experience rather than a concept. Violence, in this framework, survives through systems, habits, documents, buildings, borders, and bodies that continue carrying its consequences after the visible event has passed. Atrición makes persistence feel physical. The lyrics work through archives, silence, trauma, and accountability without collapsing into slogans. Nicolás favours metaphor, which gives the songs room to operate somewhere between private memory and public history. He is interested in transmission: what passes from one generation to another, what institutions preserve by omission, what a body remembers despite every attempt at erasure. The music answers with repetition so stubborn that it begins to resemble bureaucracy with a kick drum. By the end, Atrición feels like a controlled study in pressure: biological, political, historical, rhythmic. Catastrophe often advances by degrees, through small permissions and repeated injuries. He builds music for that recognition, and the result is frightening precisely because it moves with such discipline, until pressure itself becomes its own evidence. Listen to Atrición below and order the EP here. Atrición by Santiago Nicolás Nicolás has spent more than a decade moving through electronic music, noise, experimental composition, and post-punk, including work with The Deadly Affair, Access Device, Ángel de la Guarda, and Föllakzoid’s live lineup. Atrición compresses that experience into a language of hard surfaces and accumulating force. The production is clean enough to expose every impact, yet abrasive enough to keep the record from becoming sterile. Follow Santiago Nicolás: Bandcamp Instagram The post Chilean Techno-Industrial Producer Santiago Nicolás Performs an Autopsy on Trauma in “Atrición” EP appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 这张EP诞生于肿瘤中心附近，尼科拉斯将身体的病变逻辑与政治暴力、边境、档案及代际创伤并置，发现它们共享同一种缓慢侵蚀与占据的进程。音乐层面，他以DAF和Nitzer EBB式的经济化鼓击锚定节奏，合成器则保持冷峻前推的techno动态，同时吸收Suicide的重复结构、Cabaret Voltaire将机械转化为社会工具的思路，以及Schwefelgelb那种被截断的身体冲动。制作干净到足以暴露每一次撞击，鼓声与失真打击层在循环中逐渐加码，当重复不再像回响而像压力本身时，音乐变得真正具有攻击性。歌词以隐喻而非口号处理档案、沉默与问责，探讨创伤如何在制度、习惯、文档与身体中延续。整张作品呈现为一份关于压力的控制性研究：生物、政治、历史与节奏层面的压力，在纪律化的推进中成为自身的证据。

items.album: Bringing down the walls of Jericho
items.excerpt: And when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat… -The Book Of Joshua, Chapter 6, Verse 5 Today we’re looking at two albums featuring saxophonists whose playing could bring down the walls of Jericho. Don Dietrich and Martin Escalante aren’t interested in melody in any ordinary sense of the term. You won’t find a cover of Surrey With The Fringe On Top here.
items.body: And when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat… -The Book Of Joshua, Chapter 6, Verse 5 Today we’re looking at two albums featuring saxophonists whose playing could bring down the walls of Jericho. Don Dietrich and Martin Escalante aren’t interested in melody in any ordinary sense of the term. You won’t find a cover of Surrey With The Fringe On Top here. They are living entirely on the very edge of what their instruments can do, skronking, screeching, howling, maybe a made-up verb with -ing on the end should go here. You won’t come away from these albums humming. But if you can find yourself in the same headspace as these musicians, you will come away from listening to this stunning, frequently shocking music exhilarated. Richard Cook and Brian Morton, in writing The Penguin Guide To Jazz, used the word “god-bothering” several times. I’m not sure they meant it as a compliment, but I take it as one. I frequently think of it when I listen to music like this. This music certainly isn’t for everyone, even among free jazz fans. But for those looking for extremity in their music, these albums are special. Dietrichs - Live Bahdu (Relative Pitch, 2026) First up is Live Bahdu by the Dietrichs. Don Dietrich, along with Jim Sauter and Donald Miller, formed the thunderous free jazz/harsh noise band Borbetomagus. Rather than sitting around trying to think of new adjectives to describe Borbetomagus, I would just urge you to check them out. They aren’t on Bandcamp, but there are many samples of their music on Youtube. (True story. I was once on a jazz open discussion group when someone wrote in asking for recommendations for music similar to Chuck Mangione. Some evil person who was not me, I swear, suggested Borbetomagus. I’ve often wondered what became of that poor listener.) Here we have Don joined by his daughter Camille Dietrich on cello. While this album has much of what you would expect from an album with Don Dietrich, Camille’s cello provides an exciting counterpoint to Don’s saxophone. She’s equally skilled at plucking and bowing, her classical music training brings moments of peace and musicality and then her desire to wreak musical mayhem takes over. Don responds and the result is some serious fire and brimstone. There’s a moment just before the 4-minute mark when there is some relative calm, and then the duo turns on a dime to create a shocking racket. The whole album is full of such surprises. Live Bahdu by Dietrichs Max Devereaux & Martin Escalante - Consequences Live! (Caresse Cassettes, 2026) And then there’s Martin Escalante. Another frequent creator of extreme sounds, Mats Gustafsson, said of Escalante: “This is the JAZZ we need! URGENT! DEDICATED! RADICAL! Unique-face-peeling-cutting-edge- and-totally-in-your-face-MF! This is ALL we need for a better living!” Who am I to argue with Mats Gustafsson, especially when he’s writing in ALL-CAPS? You might think Mats is exaggerating, but a listen to this album will tell you otherwise. Escalante, especially when he’s accompanied by a guitar, sounds punk as hell to me. I’m taken back to college days when I would crash off the walls of my dorm room screaming along to Black Flag. On this release he’s accompanied by the guitar of Max Devereaux, who manages to hold his own amid the noise and haste. He’s capable of creating his own ruckus but also quite good at providing accompaniment to Escalante on his wildest flights. At times he sounds like a rhythm section and at times he sounds like a machine gun. I wasn’t familiar with him before this album, and have been checking out his work since getting it. I hope to write more about him in the future. Consequences Live! by Max Devereaux & Martin Escalante Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / extreme improvisation / noise / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 乐评聚焦两张以极端即兴为核心的专辑。Dietrichs的《Live Bahdu》由Borbetomagus成员Don Dietrich与女儿Camille Dietrich合作，父子（女）以萨克斯与大提琴展开对话，Camille的古典训练带来短暂的宁静，随后被双方共同制造的音乐混乱打破，形成平静与爆裂的骤然切换。Escalante的《Consequences Live!》延续其一贯的激进风格，萨克斯吹奏被Mats Gustafsson形容为'独特、激进、剥皮般锋利'的即兴。两位萨克斯手都不追求旋律，而是将乐器推至性能极限，制造咆哮、尖啸与刺耳声响。乐评引用《约书亚记》'城墙倒塌'的意象，暗示这类音乐具有摧毁性的力量。两张专辑分别由小厂牌Relative Pitch和Caresse Cassettes发行，适合追求听觉极端体验的听众。

items.body: SIRIUS is not a soundtrack that tries to justify its existence beyond the material it was originally created for. What Noah Rosa does is to open it up as a conversation with different artists. A cold wintry tone introduces the album. A glacial wind sweeps through. The score unfolds through slow transformations with harmony moving almost imperceptibly, but it is the dialogue between Habib El Bardi’s alto saxophone and Ruiqi Wang’s voice that gives the album its emotional centre. El Bardi’s saxophone drifts in and out of the texture with carefully judged restraint, while Wang’s voice functions as another timbral presence, dissolving into the surrounding electronics. Together they create music that feels suspended. That sense of openness is no accident. In the following interview, Noah Rosa explains that he gave both performers little more than a framework within which to improvise, allowing their own personalities to shape the music. One can hear that freedom throughout the score. Rather than sounding meticulously controlled, these pieces retain a quiet unpredictability, as though they are continually discovering themselves as they unfold. The second half of the album takes the project in a different, yet entirely coherent, direction. Rosa invited four artists to create what he calls “Refractions.” The title is more than a metaphor. These are not remixes but new perspectives on the same material, each revealing something that remained latent in the original. Vaiu’s contribution is perhaps the clearest example of this philosophy. Knowing her practice, centred on “the music underneath an instant” and on voice, time and technology as collaborators, makes perfect sense of her approach. She works from within the composition, drawing attention to tiny gestures, and the act of breathing itself. The refraction by Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das is the album’s most transformative moment. His introduction of a quiet harmonium pulse reorganises the music from within, while fragments of the original score drift in and out of focus. Nothing feels imposed. Instead, the composition reveals another possible version of itself and, in the process, goes somewhere entirely different. Ioannis Nafpliotis pushes the material further towards electroacoustic abstraction, reducing much of the score to resonance, drone and silence, before Noah Rosa himself closes the cycle with his own “Refraction.” Rather than bringing everything full circle, Rosa acknowledges the creative dialogue established by the preceding reinterpretations. His own “Refraction” expands the sonic palette, making it more luminous and harmonically warmer. The collaborative spirit of the project extends beyond the “Refractions.” Habib El Bardi, Ruiqi Wang and the three artists behind the “Refractions” are not simply invited to decorate pre-existing compositions; they become co-authors of the record. That openness seems central to Rosa’s wider practice. Across The Radiant Tower, Drawing a Circle, The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness and now SIRIUS, he repeatedly returns to ideas of grief, transformation and renewal. As he explains, music is both his way of processing personal experience and of engaging with the world beyond himself. By the end, SIRIUS has become a conversation. To discuss further the production process for the album we spoke directly with Noah Rosa. Sirius began as a film score, but the album expands beyond the boundaries of the film through the four “Refraction” pieces. When you revisited the material after the film’s completion, what were you hoping to discover in the source recordings, and how did the soundtrack transform once it was allowed to exist as a standalone work rather than serving the image? Working on the score with the director Jean-Bastien was such a great experience and I really admired and connected with his vision for the film. Also getting to work with talented friends is such a gift so bringing on Habib and Ruiqi made the whole process feel special. After the film did its festival run I had gotten some good feedback on the music, it received a socan award, and I enjoyed listening to it, so we talked about putting out the soundtrack. I’d never done this before as I think of my composing work as pretty separate from my solo releases and also generally think that film music works best in the context it was created for. So with this in mind, I was more interested in re-approaching the music as a new entity and bringing new life to it. There was some music we made when initially building the sound language for the film that wasn’t used in the edit that I was excited to share. The film is really beautifully minimal and we wanted to pare back the music as much as possible to leave the stillness and quiet that it needed to hit right. So I did a new mix of all the cues to make them a bit more present for this release and during this process I thought it would be interesting to see how some other artists might respond to the material as I felt the raw elements from Habib and Ruiqi held a sort of integrity, and were imbued with the emotion of the film. I’m really grateful to evo-natura for supporting this project and Ioannis for contributing a track. I’ve always felt he understood what I was trying to do with both SIRIUS and my previous release Two Headed Dragon and I’m really happy to have it be the home for these works. Across releases such as The Radiant Tower, Drawing a Circle, The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness, and now Sirius, there seems to be a recurring interest in grief, transformation, spirituality, and the possibility of renewal. The Radiant Tower was conceived as a mourning album and “a eulogy to the old world,” while Drawing a Circle explored cycles of collapse and endurance, and The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness emerged from notions of suffering, forgiveness, and rebirth. Looking back across these works, do you see them as chapters of a larger artistic inquiry, or has each release represented a distinct attempt to process a particular moment in your life? Music is really my best language for processing what’s around me and further, my way to engage with the world. So both are true, all the works are personal and integrate processes I’m going through in my personal life but they also all hopefully work towards a greater truth beyond me. I’m very interested in transformation, change is often what we both want and fear the most… but it’s happening regardless. The album is shaped by collaboration at several levels: from Habib El Bardi’s alto saxophone and Ruiqi Wang’s voice in the original score to the contributions of artists such as Vaiu, Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das, and Ioannis Nafpliotis in the “Refractions.” What were you looking for in these collaborators, and were there aspects of the material that surprised you when filtered through other artists’ sensibilities—particularly in the richly transformative “Refraction II” by Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das? This is definitely one of the most collaborative projects I’ve released. Ruiqi and Habib are both incredible improvisers and I really only gave them scaffolding to work within. So much of their voice and personality comes through the music and I really think of it as a shared work. For the refractions I was interested in seeing how the raw elements could be completely recontextualized into these artists’ own sound worlds. I gave very little feedback or direction for them, mostly because these artists are all just incredible, but also because I wanted to be surprised by where they took it. Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das is an artist I’ve admired for years. The way he’s able to move between long form minimalist drone and blown out idm with it making complete sense, the visual language, and sense of humour, all make him a really exciting artist. So I had no idea what to expect from the rework and loved how it brought this constant pulse from the harmonium while different layers from the score drift in and out. Similarly, when I first heard Vaiu’s track I was blown away by how she played in the musical landscape of the score but created something completely original, weaving her voice and sensibilities into the world. One striking aspect of your work is the way environmental sound, mythology, spirituality, and political reality coexist without ever feeling forced together. Both Drawing a Circle and Sirius direct their proceeds toward Palestinian causes, while albums such as The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness engage deeply with place, memory, and cultural exchange. What motivates your decision to connect these releases to concrete forms of solidarity, and do you see artistic practice as having a particular ethical responsibility in moments of ongoing crisis? I guess these are just reflections of what I care about, what I’m thinking about. I’m not making enough from music to live off anyways so I have a job to support myself. Proceeds from my releases could be supplementary to me or perhaps something a little more meaningful to someone else. It can feel a bit strange attaching monetary worth to art for me, so offering it as a gift in exchange for wealth redistribution feels more in balance. I believe all art making is political, and I hope my work carries some message of compassion and solidarity. It can also be quite a selfish and individualist thing to spend all your time trying to express your interior world so I think anything we can do to offset that by reconnecting with the world is important. Apart from artistic practice, I think we as humans all have a responsibility to reduce as much suffering as we can in our short times on this earth, or at the very least try not to add more. That is what ripples into eternity. Several of your releases—including Drawing a Circle and Sirius—have donated proceeds to Palestinian initiatives such as Grassroots Al-Quds and The Sameer Project. At a time when many artists feel pressure either to remain silent or to make overt political statements, how do you think about the relationship between sound, empathy, and action? Can ambient and experimental music contribute meaningfully to solidarity, even when it contains no explicit political message? If we are scared to even speak out about the greatest injustices happening in the world, the empires have already won. No career, status marker, or opportunity is worth turning a blind eye. I think the most important thing is patient everyday resistance and it requires constant attention. That being said I think we look to artists a little too much for their politics and social stance. Someone whose job it is to dream and play make believe might not always have the most grounded worldview. I really appreciate you asking these questions, even though I might not yet have the words to fully express what they mean to me. On a good day, I believe in music’s power to connect us with the ineffable and remind us that we are all manifestations of the same unity. Other days I think we might need less poetry and more direct action.. For now I’m just trying to be a decent person and stay connected to what matters. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body:
Required listening for computer music freaks, 'Synthesized Voices' originally appeared in 1976, collecting innovative composer Charles Dodge's prophetic vocal experiments - recordings of Mark Strand's surrealist poems recreated on Bell Laboratories' uncanny synthetic speech tech. If you're into Anton Bruhin's deranged 'Speech Poems', this'll hit the spot.

You've got to applaud DINTE for the timing of this one. Right now, it's hard to tell what's a real voice and what's been cobbled together using LLM tech, Frankensteined from decades of scraped voiceovers and newsreels. Synthesized voices are stapled to short form content and used to provide an air of humanity to mass-generated robo-slop. And listening to Dodge's set of pioneering studies, it's remarkable how the technology has evolved in such a short period of time. In the early '70s, when Dodge began his investigations, heavily synthesised voices were terrifyingly mechanical, usually used to depict malign forces - just cop any of those vintage Doctor Who episodes that feature Cybermen. What's fascinating is that Dodge seems to understand its crucial limitation; he doesn't attempt to make the voice sound more human (and therefore more tolerable), but mirrors Strand's absurdist logic instead, going beyond the limit of the larynx.

Dodge explains that he labels it computer music because it's the Bell Labs computer setup that analysed and synthesised the voices, but he's quick to say that it's not generative music. Each poem was recorded to tape first then fed into the mainframe, that was then able to recreate the language using a pre-loaded archive of words and phrases. This would have resulted in a dry study, so Dodge tested the limits of the system by reconfiguring the parameters beforehand, shifting the pitch contour, the formants and duration of the syllables to radically diverge from the way we actually speak. The eight-minute 'In Celebration' is a great starting point. Composed in 1975, it seemingly shreds Strand's poem of the same name, in actuality locating its spirit, hanging on the word "you" just like Strand does. Dodge works with speed and pitch radically, twisting the phrases into machine-gunned barrages or disorienting decelerated harmonies. The words are still there - "your lungs prepare themselves for an ashen feeling" is a banger - but they've become hoarse, noisy growls or synthetic cries. 

The four part 'Speech Songs' is lighter, rooted in poems that were intended to invite audiences to respond with laughter, yet there's something even more disturbing about a computerised voice noisily bellowing out the same word, stuttering and getting stuck on throwaway rhymes. Really, Dodge hits his stride with the ambitious 'The Story of Our Lives', an "operatic dialogue for male and female synthetic voices" that we'd love to think Robert Ashley heard. There's a similar commitment to breaking down the formula of theater and opera on display here as Dodge corrupts these mundane utterances, forcing out near-songs and high drama from soap opera-ready domestic situations. With Dodge at the controls, the words shift haphazardly from recognizable to horrifyingly alien for almost no reason whatsoever, adding a sense of danger to what might regularly be daytime telly. It's an astute skewering of American culture that's maybe more relevant now than it ever was.

items._cn_summary: 这张1976年的专辑收录了Charles Dodge在贝尔实验室合成语音技术上的开创性实验，将Mark Strand的超现实主义诗歌通过计算机重新演绎。Dodge将诗歌先录至磁带再输入主机，利用预加载的词库重构语言，并通过调整基频、共振峰和音节时长等参数，使合成声音远离人类正常发声方式。《In Celebration》中对"you"一词的反复处理极为精彩，语速与音高的极端操控将诗句撕裂为机器般的咆哮。《Speech Songs》系列中计算机声音的卡顿与重复制造出独特的荒诞感。《The Story of Our Lives》以男女合成声音构建歌剧式对话，打破传统剧场范式。整张专辑是计算机音乐与语言艺术融合的里程碑式作品。

items.body: In February of 2025, the trio of bassist Luke Stewart, drummer Chad Taylor, and trumpet-playing-electronics-wizard Aymeric Avice gathered in Studio Sextan-La Fonderie in Malakoff, France to make this exciting recording for RogueArt. Having recently performed at Périscope in Lyons, France with drummer Ramon Lopez, Stewart and Avice clearly had chemistry, and would continue to play together with both Lopez and Taylor, including a September 2025 show at the Sons d’hiver festival, a fifteen destination event orbiting Paris that focuses on experimental music, that year operating under the theme of Great Black Music . Check out part of that show here. Deep in the Earth, High in the Sky is a high-energy event. I used the word “exciting” above I think to refer more to how I feel when I listen to the music than to any specific innovation on the part of the trio during this recording. Stewart and Taylor have clearly established themselves as two of THE masters on their respective instruments on the experimental music scene, and here they display sharp and deeply communal listening as they lock-in or open-up with near ESP levels of communication. A good example of this takes place around the three-minute mark of “Pangea Suite #1,” as the two transmute a funk-oriented rock feel into a free improvisation that defies any kind of circular rhythm. Taylor seems to hit his ride cymbal just one time outside of the established backbeat and the two musicians instantaneously take off together into realms unknown. Aymeric Avice, for his part, is just so much fun to listen to, and I fear that I have slept on this musician. Avice is a trumpet virtuoso who lives and plays in electro-sonic amusements. He spends much of his time on this recording swirling and bending the pitches of his trumpet using electronic effects. And, thanks to Avice’s electronic experimentation, often these trumpet pitches come in harmonies wild, fierce, or even a little frightening. “Pangea Suite #2,” for instance features space-age trumpet electronics that can make the listener feel like they are floating in a slightly unreal ether. Check out the three-minute-ish section of this song to hear this levitation. The album is clearly conceived and follows an organized layout. The opening song is “Deep in the Earth,” book-ended by the closing composition “High in the Sky.” Both of these works feature Chad Taylor and Luke Stewart on mbira and are a lovely and meditative introduction and conclusion to the album as a whole. In between these works lie three suites: Pangea Suite , Unknown Suite , and Escaped Sounds , all of which feature the exciting interplay of drums and bass and the electro-experiments of Avice mentioned above. To my ears, the album has two clear reference points. The first is Live-Evil or Bitches Brew era Miles Davis. There are moments in the Unknown Suite , for example, that if cyphoned in ten-second snippets, could have been lifted right from one of these Miles records. “Unknown Suite #2” around 7:30 or 7:40 is evidence of this. The other unmistakable reference point is jaimie branch. jaimie’s mark is all over this album. I mean, goodness, listen to the same song just before and just after the section I referenced above. Avice’s somehow both soft and sinister distortion on the trumpet around six minutes into “Unknown Suite #2” reminds me so much of sections of fly or die. This is to say nothing of the opening of “Unknown Suite #3,” with its ebullient toms, optimistic bass line and trumpet soaring overhead. Even the opening “Deep in the Earth” uses meditative mbira playing reminiscent of some of the beautiful breezy’s work. Of course, part of this connection is because the drummer on this record IS the fly or die drummer. Deep in the Earth, High in the Sky is a fun record to listen to, and is filled with kinetic energy and intuitive interplay. At times serene and moving and at others scorched-earth electronic, this is an album worth checking out. Deep in the Earth, High in the Sky can be found here DEEP IN THE EARTH HIGH IN THE SKY by LUKE STEWART - CHAD TAYLOR - AYMERIC AVICE Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由贝斯手Luke Stewart、鼓手Chad Taylor与小号兼电子乐手Aymeric Avice在法国Malakoff的Studio Sextan-La Fonderie录制，由独立厂牌RogueArt发行。专辑以"Deep in the Earth"开篇、"High in the Sky"收尾，两首作品使用姆比拉琴，营造冥想氛围；中间三组套曲则充满贝斯与鼓的即兴对话与小号电子音效实验。小号手将传统乐器与电子处理结合，产生盘旋、扭曲、近乎超现实的音色层次。Stewart与Taylor展现出极高默契，能在摇滚律动与自由即兴之间瞬间切换，演奏中带有Miles Davis《Bitches Brew》时期的影子。整张专辑结构清晰，兼具实验精神与可听性，既扎根于自由爵士传统，又通过电子手段拓展声音边界。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)
items.label: Analog Africa
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了Antoine Dougbé与Orchestre Poly-Rythmo在1977至1982年间的创作，呈现贝宁vodun仪式传统与西非放克律动的深度融合。Dougbé以腿部拍击Cavacha节奏作为音乐传递方式，其创作带有强烈的仪式感和个人控制力。乐评指出，相比该乐队其他合辑，古巴son的影响在此更为显著，同时刚果rumba的律动也贯穿其中。曲目如《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》以合成器铺底，闪烁的吉他音色与密集踩镲节奏交织；《We Tayi Sin Assi Tche》则通过持续牛铃、鼻音呼应与紧凑重复段展现更直白的古巴根源。录音和乐器音色带有明显的时代痕迹，合成器的使用为传统节奏增添了新的层次。该专辑以独特的地域文化视角和跨风格融合，成为理解贝宁放克与伏都教音乐脉络的重要文献。

items.body: Nicolas Ladoux returns as IKKo with Cheerleader, a five-track release that continues his exploration of neo-industrial electronics through a distinctly European lens. Ladoux absorbs post-punk spirit into contemporary industrial frameworks Nicolas Ladoux returns as IKKo with Cheerleader, a five-track release that continues his exploration of neo-industrial electronics through a distinctly European lens. EBM traditions underpin the record, but these tracks never settle into simple nostalgia. Instead, Ladoux navigates shifting moods with a restrained confidence, allowing atmosphere and physicality to coexist. His voice is rarely treated as a conventional lead. Rather, it functions as another instrument of intent, communicating through cadence, tone and tension as much as words. Across the release, the emotional palette is painted in shades of silver, black and white, balancing mechanical precision with flashes of vulnerability. The production remains taut throughout. Pumping low-end bass rolls beneath surges of white noise, while drums land with the hard, disciplined impact of Front 242 and Nitzer Ebb-inspired rhythms. Fleeting acid figures bubble into view before dissolving back into the machinery, adding movement without distracting from the record’s industrial core. Closing duties fall to Velvet Underwear, whose remix drives the material further towards brutalist architecture, amplifying its weight and severity while preserving the original’s sense of disciplined restraint. Throughout Cheerleader, echoes of John Lydon‘s Public Image Ltd. emerge in the stark vocal phrasing and confrontational minimalism, yet Ladoux never slips into imitation. Instead, he absorbs that post-punk spirit into a contemporary industrial framework, resulting in a focused, stylish statement that understands the enduring power of tension over excess. Cheerleader is available on Roulette Rekordz. [Bandcamp] Cheerleader by IKKoThe post IKKo :: Cheerleader EP (Roulette Rekordz) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 这张EP以欧洲视角重新审视新派工业电子，将后朋克的冷峻骨架注入当代工业框架。Ladoux将人声视为与合成器、鼓机并列的乐器，通过节奏与张力而非歌词本身传递情绪。制作层面，低频贝斯线强劲推动，白噪声浪与硬朗节拍交织，酸性合成器旋律短暂浮现后迅速溶解回机械化的结构中。整体色调呈现银、黑、白的冷峻质感，在机械精度与脆弱感之间寻找平衡。John Lydon式的Public Image Ltd.影响隐约可闻，但作品避免了简单模仿。Velvet Underwear的混音版作为收尾，将原作推向更极端的建筑感工业领域。整张EP短小精悍，展示了作者对张力与克制的成熟控制力，是工业电子与后朋克融合领域中一次有辨识度的实践。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — From the very first notes of drums and piano, that fusion of classical music and avant-garde jazz is palpable; there is something here that breaks boundaries. As the trombone and saxophone join in to play their parts, the piano persists, seemingly indifferent to its surroundings, simply doing its own thing, and at times, it succeeds in reclaiming the spotlight. The composition speaks of something dramatic and serious, yet it avoids solemnity; it is something distinct. It is challenging, and just as one begins to digest it, the more jazz-oriented improvisational section arrives, bringing the electric guitar into the mix. Notes are exchanged between piano and guitar; they never stop playing and rewriting the rules, with so much happening simultaneously. This is the work of the Scottish group Graham Costello's Strata, featuring Costello himself on drums and Fergus McCreadie, whose classical training is clearly evident. And all of this was merely "Obelisk," the opening track.There is a structure they cannot escape, predetermined frameworks within which to move, perhaps mirroring humanity itself, or the modern and postmodern world: defined spaces for improvisation set against a predetermined beginning and end. For chaos to exist, order must come first.Another key aspect of tracks like "Stoic" or "96" is how their minimalism fuels a hypnotic pattern; on "96," Fergus McCreadie plays two distinct parts with both hands, effectively becoming, at times, a trio consisting of bass, drums, and two pianos. When the guitar enters, the atmosphere shifts to something almost cinematic, yet Joe Williamson also leans into repetitive patterns, subtly introducing variations within them.When "Jade" begins, with Costello providing drum accompaniment for Ferguson, I think of Keith Jarrett and his immense influence, an artist who, not coincidentally, was also deeply immersed in the classical world. However, the progressive dimension it acquires lies in the modal approach of the music, that European brand of minimalism that involves deliberately staying within a single scale for an extended period. And yet... the tension never flags, because the way they do it is something new. It is exciting and compels you to keep listening for more."Ocelot" evokes John Coltrane, another essential reference point, where Harry Weir's saxophone naturally takes the lead, at times breaking free; yet, thanks to the textures crafted by the piano and guitar, it soon evolves into something more... it becomes progressive jazz. It is a free-flowing symphony, executed to perfection in every detail, yet one that never loses sight of melody as a whole.The tonal palette that emerges when the guitar and trombone join forces to improvise recalls the best of early Chicago and Groove Collective, bands that, at times, seemed to have more members on stage than there were audience members watching them. Graham Costello and his band evoke the best of that era with an unmistakable timeless quality that keeps them eternally relevant.At times, the track "Sole" feels like an exercise in illustrating what it would sound like to hear sand falling in an hourglass, slow, almost imperceptible at first, then rapid and resounding as little remains toward the end. Fergus McCreadie's notes know just when to intelligently appeal to emotion and strike a deep chord; "Sapphire", meanwhile, reminded me of Morphine in its use of wind instruments with a dark, rock-tinged edge, while the piano provides accompaniment until an almost Baltic melody emerges.The cover promises a multitude of textures interwoven in a way that is modern, chaotic, yet cohesive... though that black-and-white imagery doesn't quite capture the inherent feeling, which doesn't always need to be stated explicitly. "Fly," the final track, features repetitive loops reminiscent of Stereolab alongside trombonist Steve Turre playing conch shells... yet the drums cut through, stamping the track with their own rhythm. Is it Noise rock? Post-rock? It is all of that combined with jazz, and because it blends all these elements, it becomes something distinct. It is a form of jazz that evolves and mutates, and for that very reason, it remains alive.

items.excerpt: Death has always had a public-relations problem. items.body: Death has always had a public-relations problem. We prefer it announced by thunder, church bells, skeletal hands, or some other unmistakable emblem, because ambiguity would require us to admit how easily extinction can borrow the language of consolation. On We’re Here, Washington, D.C., duo 2DCAT writes entirely from the perspective of the dead, addressing those who remain alive. On first listen, their message can sound warm: you are not alone, someone is present, and your fear will eventually lift. That reading is intentional, since 2DCAT imagines it as what the dead themselves would want us to hear. Yet the speakers from beyond the grave offer no promise of survival. They are here because they have already died, joining the largest congregation imaginable: everyone who came before us. “Fate sealed. Gates closed. A door appears. The path looks clear.” The verses trace a single account of dying, with each image marking another irreversible step. This sequence offers no metaphor for hope, recovery, or passage into a brighter phase. The dead recognize the path because they have already walked it and know where it leads. Their assurance that fear will soon be gone refers to what happens afterward, when fear disappears along with the life experiencing it. HAEZL, an opera singer whose disciplined voice gives the words an eerie composure, sings as one of those departed voices without the theatrical menace one might expect. Her restraint is essential. Death here has no need to raise its voice. Johan Hauck builds and fabricates the synthesizers used on the track, a detail that gives the music an unusually physical provenance. These machines are handmade objects producing music about the disappearance of bodies, and their cool contours provide an elegant counterweight to HAEZL’s formal poise. The arrangement draws from early European synthpop and darkwave, favoring severe textures, measured motion, and a sense of space that seems to narrow as the song proceeds. The chorus—“We’re here to remind you you’re never alone”—embodies a literal truth. Everyone who experienced the same ending still exists within this collective voice, surrounding the living as part of an immense community. The dead have always been present, and the living are simply a fleeting minority within that ongoing presence. Their companionship is genuine, not menacing: having shared the same fear, they provide the reassurance that comes from understanding how every life ultimately concludes. The video presses that claustrophobia further. Near-black frames, unstable illumination, and coarse grain reduce the visible world to fragments, as though the image itself were losing access to ordinary life. Faces and forms seem caught at the edge of perception, suspended between the unseen multitude speaking through the song and those still able to hear them. The result is less a ghost story than an encounter with inevitability, stripped of folklore and made strangely intimate. “We wouldn’t blame anyone for hearing this as hopeful,” says Hauck. “The gates being steeled, the door appearing, the path looking clear… that’s not hope. That’s dying. The dead are your guides because they’ve already made that walk.” Watch the video for We’re Here below: We’re Here belongs to a series of recent singles from 2DCAT’s forthcoming, still-unannounced album, mapping a world in collapse through several human positions: those waiting for salvation that never arrives, those retreating inward when the burden becomes unbearable, and those whose anger accelerates the destruction they fear. We’re Here supplies the voice of those who have already passed through that world. They look back upon the people still living inside it with the terrible clarity of knowing exactly how it ends. The release follows 2DCAT’s first German tour, which included dates in Leipzig, München, Berlin, and Köln’s Echoes of Rebellion festival, carrying this communion between the living and the dead into crowded rooms abroad. The We’re Here EP is out now. Order here. Follow 2DCAT: Spotify Bandcamp Instagram Facebook YouTube The post “You’re Never Alone” — The Dead Speak in DC Darkwave Duo 2DCAT’s Video for “We’re Here” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 华盛顿特区二人组2DCAT以死者的视角写就这首暗潮之作，由歌剧女声HAEZL以克制而冷静的嗓音演绎，Johan Hauck手工制作合成器提供声音骨架，呼应了关于躯体消逝的主题。编曲承袭早期欧洲合成器流行与暗潮传统，偏好冷峻音色与节制律动，空间感随歌曲推进逐渐收窄。歌词描绘死亡的不可逆过程，副歌以死者集体之声安抚生者：你们并不孤单，因为所有经历过同一终点的人仍以某种形式存在。MV采用近黑画面与粗粝颗粒感，将视觉本身也推向感知的边缘。整件作品剥离民俗叙事，以亲密而不可避免的方式直面死亡的必然性，合成器的物理质感与声乐的仪式感形成精妙平衡。

items.body:
Old pals Christina Vantzou and Félicia Atkinson reflect on coastal living on their first collaborative album, blending environmental echoes from Rome, Normandy and Hydra with mellow synth, piano, Rhodes, vibraphone, lap steel, gongs and spoken word, pulling us into the sublime.

The third chapter in RVNG's ongoing "Reflections" series, 'Water Poems' crystallises a creative relationship that began way back in 2009. Vantzou and Atkinson have performed together before, most notably in 2019 at Philharmonie de Paris, but this is the first time the duo have made a record together. Both artists live by the sea, Atkinson in Normandy on the French coast, and Vantzou in Greece, using that shared experience to power a series of hazy dream sequences filled with subtle gestures. "The sea was not taken as a monolithic postcard," Atkinson explains. "But more of a person; an energy, a mystery, a complex character we face everyday, as human beings living by the sea."

Indeed, the esoteric energy of the sea - its tides, force, majesty and hypnotic, mystical pull, is captured by the duo's eddy of electroacoustic treatments and bespoke natural soundscapes. They recorded the material in a factory on the island of Hydra in Greece, at Villa Medici in Rome and at home in their respective studios, adding expressive environmental recordings from Delphi and the Eftalou Hot Springs. The record plays like a single, hazed thought, ebbing and flowing through the same shallow waters. Words emerge and disappear into carefully processed sounds at first, before forming sentences and whole thoughts on the second side. "How can a body swim," Atkinson mouthes. "How can a person dream?"

Gorgeously, quietly seductive gear from two of the very best at this sort of thing, one to file next to Meitei's sublime 'Sen'nyū (泉涌)' from last year - recline and drift into it.
items._genre: ambient / experimental / electroacoustic / spoken word / field recording
items._cn_summary: 这是 Christina Vantzou 与 Félicia Atkinson 首次合作的专辑，隶属于 RVNG 厂牌"Reflections"系列的第三部作品。两位艺术家分别居住在法国诺曼底海岸和希腊海边，以共同的临海生活体验为创作根基，将海洋视为具有神秘能量的复杂生命体而非风景符号。专辑在希腊 Hydra 岛的工厂、罗马 Villa Medici 以及两人各自的家庭工作室录制，并融入来自德尔斐和 Eftalou 温泉的环境采样。声音层面以合成器、钢琴、Rhodes 电钢琴、颤音琴、滑棒吉他、锣与口语人声交织，配合电声处理手法，形成朦胧流动的整体氛围。前半段口语词句在精细处理的声音中若隐若现，后半段逐渐凝聚为完整的语句与思绪，模拟海潮般的呼吸节律。整张专辑如同一段绵长的意识流，持续在浅水区来回荡漾。

items.body:
Written for four Ebow-ed guitars, 'Avaeken' preserves a site-specific piece that O'Malley used to accompany an exhibition by Banks Violette. It's a microtonal symphony dedicated to Alvin Lucier and Kali Malone that's almost physically disorienting - RIYL Eleh, Phill Niblock, Pauline Oliveros et al.

It must be difficult to strike a balance when you're best known for creating some of the heaviest, most chest-pummeling drone music to ever vibrate from a stack of Sun amplifiers. But O'Malley's risen to the challenge; 'Avaeken' is relatively minimal, for him at least, but smacks with an intensity that you don't really see coming until your body starts feeling it. Made using four vibrating strings, he tunes the instruments to create that unsettling beating sound that seems to whirl around the noggin as the resonances interfere with each other. O'Malley wrote the piece following a commission from Belgium's ZWERM electric guitar quartet in 2020, performing it a handful of times before they knuckled down and recorded it in Gent's Muziekcentrum De Bijloke, a medieval hospital that's been fitted out with the proper acoustic treatments. 

And if you've been studying O'Malley's output carefully, you'll already know that he's frequently been spotted alongside Violette, the American artist best known for his huge sculptures and installations. The two have been friends for two decades at this point and have worked together multiple times, so when Violette was describing his show 'Wish You Were Here', an exhibition that tears at the fabric of America's subcultural underground, O'Malley immediately thought about this piece. The link might not be obvious, but O'Malley's use of phase cancellation - when "sound energy is eating itself", in O'Malley's own words - reaps ample rewards here. The effect is unsubtle, penetrating oscillations so disorienting that Violette's themes of societal rot emanate from every skewed tone.

O'Malley presents two takes of the same piece, fixing Violette's striking artwork - of a cracked mirror ball - to the cover. And it's incredible to hear him working as a composer for a change, letting the ZWERM quartet do the heavy lifting. Their expertise helps elevate the piece; it's precise, expertly rendered gear, the kind of thing you need to give your full attention to. Surprisingly, it's also got more in common with those Sunn O))) records than you might expect - play at high volume and you'll know exactly what we mean.
items._cn_summary: Stephen O'Malley 为四把 Ebow 电吉他创作的微音律作品，源自 2020 年比利时 ZWERM 电吉他四重奏委约，在根特中世纪医院改建的音乐厅录制。整张专辑围绕相位抵消与弦共振干涉展开，调律产生的差拍效应在空间中旋转，制造出身心失重般的声学体验。O'Malley 以作曲家身份退居幕后，将演奏全权交予四重奏执行，演奏精度极高，细节层次需要专注聆听方能捕捉。作品献予 Alvin Lucier 与 Kali Malone，并在视觉上以 Banks Violette 的裂镜球装置呼应。Sunn O))) 式的极端响度仍是底色，但表达方式更内敛、克制，低频压力在安静中缓慢积聚，是 O'Malley 创作脉络中相当独特的转折点。

items.body:
Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.
items._genre: dub techno / abstract dub / experimental electronic / dark ambient
items._cn_summary: Ghost Dubs的专辑延续了柏林抽象dub脉络，从King Tubby与Lee Scratch Perry的牙买加传统出发，经由Basic Channel旗下Rhythm & Sound、Pole以及Chain Reaction等厂牌的变体发展，将dub作为一种方法论融入techno与噪音的语境。整张专辑以颗粒化、去物质化的声音处理为核心，低频sub-bass构成稳定基底，十二首作品均笼罩在黏滞、潮湿的催眠氛围中，速度被刻意放慢，形成统一的聆听体验。从灼蚀的Chemical到肿胀涌动的Circles Lines，制作人将dub的回声、延迟与空间处理推向原子化分解的极端，同时保留了经典dub的律动骨架。Kevin Martin即The Bug对此作品有直接影响，声音在经典与当代之间游走，呈现出模糊、蒸汽态的质地，适合寻求沉浸式低音体验与声音解构的听众。

items.body:
Tyondai Braxton’s new album, his first full-length release since the recording of his 2022 symphonic work, Telekinesis, reveals itself as unlike what came before and marks the beginning of a new chapter with UK label Erased Tapes. First off, there’s a lot more music here, 70+ minutes of pure electronics and sound design. Plus, it’s divided in a way that’s out-of-step with the longer forms the 47 year-old composer/producer has previously imagined into being. Of the album’s 15 tracks, more than two-thirds are sub-five minutes.

"The album brings together mostly newer works alongside pieces composed across the past decade, some of which appeared previously as standalone releases. To fully represent the scope of this period, Braxton incorporates the Dia / Phonolydian (2022) and Multiplay (2023) singles into Splayed Werks, foregrounding the project’s long-form compositional arc. Along with “Salt Point” and previously unreleased commissioned works such as “4 Zones” (2018) and “K Space” (2021), these pieces were always part of a broader, evolving body of material. Here, they are re-edited as newer versions and remastered by the excellent Matt Colton at Metropolis Studios in London and woven into a continuous narrative. The result is not so much a compilation, but a record that traces its own lineage in real time: a body of work composed across years, now fully realized as a single, cohesive statement.

What the circumstantial facts can’t reveal is the social, in-real-life context of Splayed Werks, an expansive episodic work that plants a musical flag on a turbulent period, and on which darkness and ambiance, rhythm and light, instinct and precision, organic textures and messy playfulness all share space. These Werks take stock of a constantly evolving world, as well as the evolutions experienced by their creator.

It may be a perfect album for 2026, a time when the sonic landscape continues to fervently embrace increasingly radical hybrids, at once club soundsystem-ready, art-installation-leaning, and music-school-mediated. But also, importantly, intuitive and hand-crafted. It’s no stretch to say that Tyondai had a hand in building this world. His two decades-plus-long career has seen him co-found electronic prog-punk heroes Battles (which he’s described as “a laboratory that masqueraded as a band”); performing as a duo with Philip Glass; write numerous electro-acoustic and chamber commissions for celebrated American new-music ensembles such as Bang on a Can All-Stars, Alarm Will Sound, Third Coast Percussion, Brooklyn Rider, and Yarn/Wire; having his “part installation, part band” HIVE project appear at The Guggenheim Museum, Sydney Opera House, and a 3-night residency at Big Ears Festival; and deliver a series of technologically ambitious, at times orchestral works for lauded labels of electronic, experimental and future-music, Warp and Nonesuch Records.

Meanwhile, the world outside has also radicalized. Mechanisms behind the creation, promotion, distribution and broadcast of new experimental music have been violently disrupted, even as audiences for it have grown. In the post-COVID streaming age, juxtapositions like “popular” vs “underground,” and “album” vs “collection” vs “project” have been more in-flux than ever before. The volume and acceptance of previously neglected ambient and contemporary classical sounds has been tempered by a lack of critical context, seeded with algorithmic buffoonery and AI fabrication. Such tensions enlighten not just the make-up of Splayed Werks, full of music recorded between 2018-2025, but its relatively simple sonic-collage forms.

The Splayed shapes and structures have also been influenced by the transformations in Braxton’s personal life. That Tyondai is now a father may not come as a surprise, but the fact that the man who rebelled against his formal music-school education in the late-‘90s, has, in 2022 become a professor of music composition at Princeton University, does. This lifestyle change—a full-time academic gig, escaping the careerist hamster-wheel beholden to commissions and collaborations, a home studio as his own workshop and testing ground, with the desire to finish things and the perspective to not be precious about it—is also key to the album’s sound. Braxton’s time is his own, and his idea of what it means to be an artist in our time has evolved as much as the surroundings. This too is what Splayed Werks is about. It may be a cliché to call each ensuing album by a veteran artist their “most personal,” but it’s no stretch to say this one best reflects who Braxton is in 2026.

As a portfolio, Splayed Werks hews to the menu of a dance music meets minimalist electronic composition, a throughline that stretches from IDM absurdists like Aphex Twin and Autechre, to contemporary immersives like Mica Levi and Laurel Halo. (And, to a lesser degree, to Braxton’s comrades and occasional collaborators, Kieran “Four Tet” Hebden, Jeffrey Cantu-Ledesma and Ben Vida.) It’s a world in which the multitude of dirty rhythms strays far outside club-land’s big rooms—though one can imagine expert mixing hands and a world-class soundsystem transforming the dubwise lo-fi linearity of “Oslo” into a psychedelic wonder, while the interplay between the bass-synth and the constantly deviating shuffle on “UnFS” may qualify as a leftfield banger. And its composed beatless spaces have little to do with current ambient proclivities—the at-once aggressive and ecstatic, panning miniature, “Realistic Water” sounds like power Laraaji.

The spectrum of Braxton’s ideas and directions reveals a voracious mind at play, changing up without overcomplicating the proceedings. Two different pieces called (fittingly) “Multiplay” layer and connect skittering textures in beatwise whimsy, before giving way to a droning dread and organised noise; yet each is adorned with birdcalls to balance the synthetic with the pastoral. “Nimble FX” is also built on hyper-jittery stop-start rhythm lines, and great big cinematic synths. All this music feels fluid, seemingly ready to change in the moment rather than having been dependent on some grand design. Meanwhile, longer, older, more spacious compositions like “4 Zones,’ whose short parts assemble into a narrative-free sound design, and the closing “K Space,” whose chaotic ambiance gives way to what sound like Moog hits, are more grounded, their inclusion shaping Splayed Werks into a multidimensional space, instinctive in how it all fits together."

“Every record I’ve ever finished, I’ve been shocked with what it is. I’ve never known it was finished until it was. Then you get to learn about it retroactively. If I’ve done it right, the finished thing will feel like its own personality, its own being, its own vibe. [Splayed Werks] included.” - Tyondai Braxton

items.body:
Carrier winds the rhythmic tension to breaking point on his 4th self-released 12”, flexing fine-tuned muscle memory and inch-tight production in acres of negative space across a trio of soundsystem phantoms that dance in the long shadow of D&B and broken beat science. Huge tip FFO Autechre, Burial, Photek, T++.

Now three years into a generational run of inspirational plates - including an AOTY ’25 with ‘Rhythm Immortal’ for Modern Love - Carrier’s core sense of discipline and restraint continues to yield peerless reward on ‘Thresholds’. A lifetime’s love of, and immersion in, fwd UK dance musics has prompted him to chase a particular dragon of syncopated swerve and cavernous psychoacoustics to logical, next-level depths diffusing that dread pressure with an adroit, tendon-twitching precision and tactility.

Carrier has been instrumental in reminding ravers what was lost when D&B went stadium and pop-chart scale over the past decades, daring to run against the grain, trust his instincts, to return a sense of mystery and bold experimentalism to what was once a thrilling paradigm. This new trio of cuts eke exquisite nuance from tweaked fundamentals, swivelling 2-step off the bone into smoky hall-of-mirrors reflections of ‘Cure’, and specialising in a razor’s edge, toes-off-the-ground sorcery in a recursive, wraithlike zinger, ‘Scout’ that dips to the sexiest, tongue-tip breakdown, beside the tantric, anticipatory chicanery of ‘Black Channels’ which finishes us off with an all-tension-no-release weapon for the ages.

items._cn_summary: Carrier在其第四张自发行黑胶作品中，将节奏张力推至临界点，在大面积负空间中铺陈精密的制作与肌肉记忆般的节律控制。三首作品游走于鼓打贝斯与破碎节拍的科学脉络中，承袭Autechre、Burial、Photek的实验精神。他以多年沉浸于英国前沿舞曲的积累，追索切分节奏的蜿蜒与空旷心理声学，释放出精准而具触感的压迫感。专辑在'Cure'中以烟雾般的镜像折射拆解二步拍骨架，在'Scout'里展现悬浮于地面的锋利巫术，于'Black Channels'终曲以纯粹张力收束，回归鼓打贝斯早期的实验性与神秘气质。

items.body:
HTRK slickly seduce with the unheimlich sensuality on 'Work (Work, Work)'.

While it may be gauche to attribute the lightless mood of this LP to the departure of Sean Stewart in 2010, it certainly lends some inescapable context. It's hardly like they were doing tween-pop previously, but the sense of gloom and dystopia is almost suffocatingly closer to the edge, from the crawling-on-all-fours pacing, to the detached, androgynous vocals of Jonnine Standish and their perversely detailed production values.

They've got our attention instantly with the sideroom synth eurotica of 'Ice Eyes Eis', and sustain the mood beautifully into the pinging metallic delays and seeping reverb of 'Slo Go', sounding like a Atelecine produced by a young Geoff Barrow after a The Birthday Party binge. Dragging us further down, on 'Eat Yr Heart' the beats become clammier and more echoic, while Jonnine's vox become a ghostly vapour trail of condensed reverb. At the album's apex, 'Skinny', the beats feel like a dystrophied version of something from Mika Vainio's 'Life, It Eats You Up…' album, and 'Synthetik' serves a tangibly textured taste of steely Techno pulses and opiated post-punk guitar drifts into 'Poison'.

To close, the heavy-hearted atmopshere weighs heavier still on 'Work That Body', tracing anaesthetic connections with their Melbourne forefathers, Pelican Daughters, before the bleak romance of 'Love Triangle' and the blank-eyed writhe of 'Body Double'.

For fans of occluded sonics from Pump to Atelecine or Mika Vainio, this is a strongly recommended listen.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将暗潮的阴沉氛围推向近乎窒息的程度，乐句在爬行般的节奏中缓慢推进，人声如同幽灵般漂浮于回声与混响之中。制作上充满工业质感与金属延迟效果，合成器编织出冷色调的欧陆舞曲质感，吉他音色则带有后朋克的麻醉感。整张作品在慢速脉冲与声学质感之间构建出一种忧郁而亲密的张力，歌曲之间通过回响、延迟与纹理细节相互连接。从开场曲的欧洲合成器情色氛围，到中段的粘稠鼓机与幽灵声轨，再到尾声的工业合成器与空眼神秘主义，专辑呈现出连续的情绪下潜轨迹。乐评将这张作品置于Atelecine、Geoff Barrow、Pelican Daughters与Mika Vainio的影响光谱中，作为对遮蔽式声响美学爱好者的强烈推荐。

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.
items._genre: ambient / analog synth / drone / film score / hauntology
items._cn_summary: Mark Jenkin 为其康沃尔海员题材电影创作的合成器原声，以磁带质感的模拟合成器、深蓝潮湿的音色调色板构建海洋尺度的氛围。音乐围绕一艘无船员归港的拖网渔船展开，充满对失去与怀念的冥想气质。循环旋律与持续低音铺陈出可触的忧郁感，曲目在恍惚意识中渐入渐出，带有磁带抖动与失真效果，如锈迹与风化礁石上的盐霜。最终曲以民谣节奏消隐于地平线。整张专辑即使脱离影像也作为独立作品成立，将民间恐怖配乐传统与AMM式漂移电子相融合，是氛围与实验音乐爱好者值得关注的跨界之作。
